note: Everything the website says in its own voice. The generator in apps/press supplies no prose of its own: if a sentence appears on the site and is not a fact out of the village record, it is in this file. Directive 10 for the same reason wording lives in templates.json -- a page should be improvable by somebody who has never opened a TypeScript file. Keep it plain. Short sentences, concrete nouns, no salesmanship.
tagline: A simulation of medieval life, with a twist

home.title: Welcome to Pennycroft
home.lead: Pennycroft is a village of eighty-six people that does not exist. They wake up, walk to work, and go to bed without anybody telling them to, and this is their newspaper.

sections.heading: What this is
body: Pennycroft is a computer program pretending to be a medieval village. There are eighty-six people in it. Each one has a name, an age, a family, a house, and a job to walk to. Time moves forward one second at a time, and the program writes down everything that happens.

Nobody writes the story. If Gilbert Hollis walks to the smithy and finds it full, that is because the smithy holds six people and six people got there before him. He turns around and walks home. That is the whole of it, and it gets put in the paper, because on most days it is the most interesting thing that happens.

sections.heading: The twist
body: The village reports on itself. There is no narrator. Every day the program looks at what happened, decides what mattered, and prints a page about it. The villagers write their own short notes about their own day, and they are only allowed to mention things they were actually present for. Nobody under ten writes anything, because nobody under ten could. What one of them did still reaches the page the way it would have in a real village: a parent mentions it.
So the paper can be thin. Some days genuinely are. When the paper has nothing to say it says nothing, and there is a note at the bottom of every issue listing what it cannot tell you yet and why.

sections.heading: Everything here can be checked
body: Every sentence on this site stands on a numbered event in the village record, and the numbers are printed next to it. Nothing is added afterwards to make a day read better. If it is not in the record, it does not go on the page.

The village is also rebuildable. Give the program the same starting word and it produces the same eighty-six people living the same days in the same order, down to the second. That is what makes the record worth keeping.

towne.title: The Towne
towne.lead: Thirty-eight places, fourteen of them out of doors, joined by lanes that cost real minutes to walk.

sections.heading: Getting about
body: The village is a set of places and the roads between them. Walking from the Green to Mill Lane takes three minutes. Walking out to the North Gate takes longer. Nobody in Pennycroft can be in two places at once, and nobody arrives anywhere without walking the distance first.
Most buildings have a limit on how many people fit inside. That is not decoration. It is the single most common thing that goes wrong in the village, and the paper reports it more than anything else.

sections.heading: Who owns the map
body: The map was drawn by hand from the village file, which lists every place, its type, how many it holds, and what it connects to. If a lane is added to the file, it appears in the village, and people start using it the same day.

people.title: The People
people.lead: Eighty-six souls in twenty-four households. Each one has a face, a family, and a life the record can account for.

sections.heading: How they got their names
body: The families were written by hand — the Netherbys, the Hargraves, the Barrows, the Carters and the rest — and then the program handed out the children. A person's family is the roof they were first recorded under. Two houses of Hargraves both count as Hargraves, which is why this site counts family names and not households.

The faces are drawn, and each one is assigned to a person whose age and sex actually match it. A face is checked against the record rather than trusted: nobody wears a face of the wrong sex or the wrong stage of life, and no two people wear the same one.

sections.heading: What they can and cannot do yet
body: Right now a villager can wake, walk, work, be turned away from a full building, and go to bed. They do not yet remember anything, own anything, buy anything, marry anybody, or hold a grudge. Those arrive in later phases, one at a time, each with its own record in the paper.
Nobody in Pennycroft has died yet, of anything. When that changes, the paper will be the first to say so.

paper.title: The Chronicle
paper.lead: One page a day, written out of the village record. The day in review, a count of how the village stood at midnight, and an honest note about what is still missing.

blog.title: The Villagers
blog.lead: Short notes from the people themselves. A villager may only write about something they were standing next to when it happened, which is why some days they have nothing to say. The youngest are too small to write anything down, so when one of them turns up here it is a parent mentioning them.

about.title: About Pennycroft
about.lead: How the village works, what it can prove, and what it is still pretending about.

sections.heading: One second at a time
body: The simulation keeps a clock and a queue of things waiting to happen. A villager decides what to do, the program works out how long it takes, and puts them down for that many seconds later. A day is eighty-six thousand four hundred ticks, and a tick is a second.

Every change of any importance is written down as a numbered event: who did it, where, when, and what caused it. A month of the village is about eighty megabytes of those events. That pile is a cache, not a record — it can be deleted and rebuilt from the starting word whenever it is wanted.

sections.heading: What gets kept forever
body: Out of those millions of events, a small number are worth remembering next year. Those get boiled down to three plain text files: everyone who has ever existed, everywhere that exists, and one line per day for everything that mattered. A year of village memory is a few hundred kilobytes and can be read in a text editor.
That is the part a seed cannot rebuild, because it is a judgement rather than a fact. It is also the part this website is printed from.

sections.heading: The rules it holds itself to
body: A villager may only act on something they could actually know. Money, food, goods and people cannot appear out of nowhere. Nothing crosses the map without walking it. The program never uses the computer's clock or an unseeded coin flip, because either one would mean the same village could not be rebuilt twice.

There is no artificial intelligence in the simulation. None of the villagers' decisions are made by a language model, and the village runs with no internet connection at all. The pictures on this site were drawn with an image model and are illustrations, not evidence — everything with a number next to it came out of the record.

sections.heading: What is missing on purpose
body: The paper has no author, because nobody in Pennycroft can read or write yet. There are no classified notices, because there is no money. Nothing continues from yesterday, because nobody has a relationship the record can prove. Nobody remembers anything, so the page can tell you what was done and never why.
Each of those is a phase of work with a place in the plan, and each one is named at the bottom of every issue of the paper. A gap that is written down is a gap somebody can close.

footer: Pennycroft is a simulation. Nobody named on this site is a real person, living or dead.
The village is rebuilt from a single starting word, so every page here can be produced again from scratch and come out the same.
